### Description
In `DataFrame.to_xml()`, boolean columns were formatted using plain `str()` in `_build_elems` and `_build_attribs`, producing capitalized `"True"` and `"False"`. These values do not validate against XML Schema `xs:boolean`, which requires lowercase `"true"` and `"false"`.

This PR introduces `_get_xml_value` in `_BaseXMLFormatter` to serialize boolean types (`bool`, `np.bool_`) to `"true"` and `"false"` while preserving other types and missing value handling. Regression tests covering element and attribute outputs for standard, NumPy, and nullable boolean series were added.

title: TST: pin non-unitary anchored resample offset phase behavior (GH#29576)
body:
## What does this PR do?

Follow-up to #64425, which was closed after review showed the proposed fix was a no-op.

- Pins the current, intentional behavior of `resample()` with a non-unitary anchored offset (e.g. `"2QS-MAR"`): the previous bin edge comes from `BaseOffset.rollback`, which steps back exactly one offset regardless of the offset's own stride, so the bin phase tracks where the data starts rather than being fixed by `startingMonth`. This is uniform across non-unitary `MS`/`QS`/`YS` offsets, not a quarter-only quirk, and had no test coverage (the issue's `Needs Tests` label).
- Pins `HalfYearBegin`/`HalfYearEnd` (`HYS`/`HYE`, added in #60946) as the offsets that do anchor on `startingMonth` regardless of data start, which is the behavior #29576 originally asked for.
- Adds a `See Also` cross-reference from `QuarterBegin`/`QuarterEnd` to `HalfYearBegin`/`HalfYearEnd` for anyone who hits the same non-unitary-quarter surprise.

Related to #29576. No behavior change, so no whatsnew entry.

## Test command

- `pytest pandas/tests/resample/test_datetime_index.py -k "non_unitary_anchored_offset_phase or half_year_offset_anchors"`
- `pytest pandas/tests/resample/ pandas/tests/tseries/offsets/`

title: BUG: densifying a datetimelike SparseArray mixed pandas and numpy scalars
body:
`SparseArray.__array__` inferred the dense dtype from `np.result_type(subtype, type(fill_value))`, which gives `object` for a boxed `Timestamp`/`Timedelta` fill value and raises for `np.nan`. Densifying a datetime64/timedelta64 `SparseArray` therefore returned an object array with the stored values boxed by numpy as `datetime.datetime` (coarser units) or raw integers (nanoseconds), beside the pandas-boxed fill value — one array holding two types, neither matching the dense result. This is the half GH-68073 missed: the branch it added only fires when `object` is passed explicitly, while `astype(object)` and `Series.to_numpy()` arrive with `dtype=None`.

`to_dense()` passes the subtype explicitly and had a separate bug in the same block: it handed the fill value to `np.full`, which truncates a `Timestamp` to microseconds through the stdlib datetime protocol, and reads a fill left in another unit — the `us` a string-parsed `Timestamp` carries — as a raw integer under a numeric cast.

Both now route through the existing `_promote_for_fill` helper, which normalizes any fill spelling to a numpy scalar in the subtype's own unit; `_densify` already did this. Checked by differential against the dense result across unit, kind, fill spelling and requested dtype.

title: BUG: SparseArray truncated a boxed Timestamp/Timedelta fill_value
body:
A datetime64/timedelta64 `SparseArray` whose `fill_value` is a boxed `pd.Timestamp`/`pd.Timedelta`, rather than the `np.datetime64`/`np.timedelta64` spelling of the same value, was mishandled wherever the fill value reached numpy:

- `np.full`/`np.insert` route a boxed pandas scalar through the stdlib datetime protocol, which caps at microseconds, so `to_dense()`, `value_counts()`, `unique()` and arithmetic materialized a sub-microsecond `fill_value` as a *different* value.
- `np.result_type(sp_values.dtype, type(fill_value))` gives `object` for a boxed pandas scalar, so `np.asarray` returned `object` dtype holding the stored values unboxed — raw `int64` on a nanosecond unit — which the `Series` repr then printed in place of the values.

```python
values = np.array([1, 2, 2], dtype="i8").astype("m8[ns]")
boxed = SparseArray(values, fill_value=pd.Timedelta(1))

boxed + boxed        # fill 0, dense [2, 4, 4]      <- expected [2, 4, 4] with fill 2
boxed.to_dense()     # [0, 2, 2]                    <- expected [1, 2, 2]
np.asarray(boxed)    # array([Timedelta('...001'), 2, 2], dtype=object)
```

Rather than unbox at each site, this normalizes the fill value once in `SparseDtype.__init__` to the subtype's own numpy scalar, mirroring the `pd.NaT` normalization GH-68449 added directly above it — whose comment states the same goal, "so that the two spellings of the fill value behave identically downstream". Every route to a `SparseArray`'s fill value goes through that constructor, including the `fill_value` setter, so one line covers all of the sites above.

Placement after `_check_fill_value()` is load-bearing and pinned by a test: normalizing first would turn a tz-aware `Timestamp` into a naive `datetime64` that passes validation, silently dropping the timezone.

As with the `pd.NaT` spelling already, `fill_value` now comes back as `np.datetime64`/`np.timedelta64` rather than the boxed scalar, and the dtype repr changes accordingly. Incidentally this also makes the two spellings hash equal, where before they compared equal but hashed differently.

Overlaps with GH-68578, which fixes the same underlying bug per-site with a `_unbox_fill_value` helper. Opening this as a draft so the two can be compared rather than both landing — the differences are that this one also covers arithmetic (`_get_fill`, which GH-68578 leaves untouched) and needs no per-site wiring, while GH-68578 keeps `fill_value` boxed and additionally removes the now-dead `NaT` branch in `__array__`. Happy to close whichever we don't want.

title: BUG: unstack added a column for a level value no row used (GH#68588)
body:
`_Unstacker` assumed that after `remove_unused_levels()` every value of the unstacked level is used by some row. That is false by design — `remove_unused_levels` returns the index unpruned when a level holds NaN as a value, so the level keeps its unused NaN entry (GH-37510). That entry then got a column of its own: a duplicate NaN column under `sort=True`, and under `sort=False` a width disagreement between `get_new_values` and `get_new_columns` that raised, or on a mixed-dtype frame left blocks wider than the placements they were given.

Fix: narrow `removed_level` to the used entries under `sort=True`, renumber the level codes to match, and use one `stride` expression at all four sites (two used `levshape[level] + has_nan`, which agrees only when nothing is unused). The narrowing is gated on `any(lev.hasnans for lev in self.index.levels)`, since the GH-37510 bail-out is the only way `remove_unused_levels` returns unpruned; without the gate it cost ~7% of a 1M-row `Series.unstack`.

Found while auditing GH-64516, which removed the mask-based empty-column filtering on the strength of that assumption. That PR's Cython simplification is untouched here.

title: BUG: read_csv silently wrapped out-of-range integers (GH#55232)

labels.name: NA - MaskedArrays
labels.description: Related to pd.NA and nullable extension arrays

body:
closes #55232

Since 2.0, `read_csv` silently wrapped a value the requested integer `dtype` could not hold — `read_csv(StringIO("x\n-1\n257"), dtype={"x": "UInt8"})` returned `[255, 1]` — where the `Series` and `array` constructors raise.

Three cast sites reached the wraparound:

- `_coerce_to_data_and_mask`'s `isinstance` fastpath raw-astyped instead of calling `_safe_cast`. This is the nullable half, and the actual 2.0 regression; both engines route nullable dtypes through it. Masked slots are filled before the check, since the data behind the mask is meaningless.
- the c engine's int branch in `TextReader._convert_with_dtype`. The check is gated on `user_dtype` rather than skipped for `int64`, so a column that only fits `uint64` now raises for `dtype={"x": "int64"}` instead of coming back as `uint64` with the requested dtype ignored. Inference is unaffected — it passes `user_dtype=0` and keeps the `uint64` fallback result.
- `PythonParser._cast_types`.

Nullable dtypes raise `TypeError`, restoring the pre-2.0 message; numpy dtypes raise `ValueError`, reusing the message the parser already produces from the fallback safe-cast block in `_convert_tokens`.

With the fastpath fixed, `BaseMaskedArray._coerce_same_family` (added in GH-66332) is redundant — both call sites fall through to the identical `_coerce_to_array(..., dtype=self.dtype)` — so it is removed. That also drops its one remaining difference, which was a bug: it checked `value._data` at masked positions, so assigning an NA whose stale payload did not fit the target dtype raised.

Deliberately unchanged: `engine="pyarrow"`, which casts the parsed frame in `_finalize_dtype` (the new parser test is `@xfail_pyarrow`); `astype`, which keeps numpy semantics and belongs to GH-45588 — note `Series`/`DataFrame` construction from an existing masked array delegates to `astype`, so only `pd.array` changes there; and float-to-integer *truncation* on the python engine, which `test_read_fwf.py::test_dtype` asserts — floats are compared truncated so only wraparound raises.

This does not depend on GH-45588, which was raised on the issue as a possible prerequisite.

title: BUG: SparseArray object subtype took the truth of an elementwise comparison

labels.name: Missing-data
labels.description: np.nan, pd.NaT, pd.NA, dropna, isnull, interpolate

body:
Three `SparseArray` methods compared object-dtype values against a scalar and then took the
truth of the result. When a stored value is `pd.NA` that comparison yields `pd.NA` rather than
a bool, so each raised `TypeError: boolean value of NA is ambiguous` where the dense path
answers normally:

```python
arr = SparseArray(np.array([1, pd.NA, 0, 1], dtype=object), fill_value=0)

arr == 0                       # TypeError; dense gives [False, False, True, False]
arr.value_counts(dropna=False) # TypeError; dense gives {1: 2, <NA>: 1, 0: 1}
arr.map(lambda x: x)           # TypeError; dense gives [1, <NA>, 0, 1]
```

- `value_counts` built its fill mask with `keys == self.fill_value`, then called `mask.any()`
- `_cmp_method` assigned `op(self.sp_values, other)` into an `np.bool_` buffer
- `map` tested `new_sp_val == fill_val`

An `object` subtype now goes through the same NA-aware kernels the non-sparse path uses
(`ops.comparison_op` / `ops.comp_method_OBJECT_ARRAY`), mirroring the dense fallback
`_logical_method` already has, and `map` skips the collision check for a missing scalar.

Three neighbouring defects fall out of the same route and are in the whatsnew:

- two `object` subtype operands with different sparse indices raised `AttributeError: module
  'pandas._libs.sparse' has no attribute 'sparse_eq_object'` even with no NA present, because
  `splib` has no object kernel
- a missing scalar such as `None` was reported equal to a stored `None`, where dense reports
  `False`; ordering operators against a missing scalar raised rather than answering all-`False`
- a nullable `boolean` operand is now deferred to via `NotImplemented`, so it keeps its own NA
  instead of being densified. Without that guard the new dense route would have turned a loud
  raise into a silent `False`

The comparison scalar arm works off `sp_values` rather than materializing the array, which also
makes it faster than before: 0.019 ms vs 0.424 ms on main for `arr == 1` at 1e6 elements with
100 stored.

Note for review: GH-68579 (draft) touches `_cmp_method` as well. It adds the same
`NotImplemented` guard but for *every* masked dtype, and splits a shared `_cmp_or_logical_op`
out of `_cmp_method`. This PR is deliberately standalone — without its own guard it would
introduce the silent-`False` regression described above — so whichever lands second should drop
the now-redundant guard, and the `is_cmp` flag here becomes unnecessary once the logical fast
path stops routing through `_cmp_method`.

tests and ran a multi-round blind self-review over the diff.

title: DOC: document the extension-dtype behavior change from GH#61828

labels.name: Testing
labels.description: pandas testing functions or related to the test suite

labels.name: ExtensionArray
labels.description: Extending pandas with custom dtypes or arrays.

body:
GH-61828 enabled `fill_value` for `DataFrame`-with-`Series` flex ops by deleting the `else: return series` early-out in `_maybe_align_series_as_frame`. That has a much wider blast radius than its whatsnew entry (which mentions only `fill_value`) suggests: along the default `axis="columns"`, an extension-dtype right operand is now broadcast and run through the blockwise path instead of being dispatched element-by-element as scalars, which changed

- the result dtype (`Int64` rather than `int64`, `boolean` rather than `bool`),
- the result *values* wherever NA is involved — `df > Series([1, None], dtype="Int64")` used to give `False` in the NA column and now gives `NA`,
- and which operations raise: arithmetic and ordering comparisons against a `category` Series used to operate on the categories as if they were plain scalars, and now raise `TypeError` the way `Series`-with-`Series`, `DataFrame`-with-`DataFrame`, and `Categorical`-with-scalar always did. Conversely a few operations that raised spuriously, such as adding an integer frame to a `period` Series, now succeed.

Logical `&`/`|`/`^` travel the same path (`_logical_method is _arith_method`), as do `Index` and bare `ExtensionArray` right operands. `axis=0` was already behaving this way and is unchanged.

This adds an `Other API changes` entry for all of it, plus regression tests. No test covered a `DataFrame` operated against an extension-dtype `Series` at all, which is why the change shipped through green CI; all four new tests fail if GH-61828 is reverted.

No source change. This started as a follow-up to an audit finding that called the `category` works-to-raises a regression to be fixed before 3.1; on investigation the new behavior is the correct one — `DataFrame`-with-`Series` was the only box in which Categorical arithmetic succeeded, and only because the dtype never reached the operation — so the finding was closed as `wontfix` and the gap turned out to be documentation and test coverage.

title: BUG: read_json(orient="table") could not read back non-string labels (GH#19129)
body:
closes #19129

The issue title asks for a `ValueError`, but on current main the symptom is worse than the 2018 report: an ordinary frame with default `RangeIndex` columns round-trips through `orient="table"` to all-NaN with no error at all.

```python
df = pd.DataFrame([[1.5, 2.5], [3.5, 4.5]])
pd.read_json(StringIO(df.to_json(orient="table")), orient="table")
#     0   1
# 0 NaN NaN
# 1 NaN NaN
```

An int-dtype frame instead raises `IntCastingNaNError` naming a column that "does not exist", as does a non-string index name; a `MultiIndex` with a non-string level name raises `AttributeError: 'int' object has no attribute 'startswith'` on the *write* side.

The schema field `name` is JSON-serialized from the label, so an int label stays the JSON number `5`, while the record keys in `"data"` are `str(label)` (`"5"`). `parse_table_schema` looked the data up by the schema name and matched nothing.

So this makes the labels round-trip rather than rejecting them. Matching is done on the field name's string form, with the original labels restored at the end. Field names are metadata rather than data, so the schema is re-read at full precision when one of them is a float — otherwise the fast parser perturbs `0.3` into `0.30000000000000004` and the match fails for a perfectly ordinary frame. Two cases genuinely cannot be recovered and now raise `ValueError` instead of reading as NaN: a label whose string form matches no key (a float written with too small a `double_precision`), and two distinct labels that share a string form (`5` and `"5"`).

Two write-side fixes come along because the round-trip needs them: `set_default_names` is guarded against a non-string `MultiIndex` level name, and a falsy `Series` name (`0`, `False`, `""`) is no longer replaced by the `"values"` placeholder — only a `None` name is a missing name.

Not addressed here, and left for a follow-up on the write side: `None`, tuple, and duplicate labels still emit a schema `name` that disagrees with the data keys. The full remedy is to derive the schema `name` from the same stringification the C writer uses for object keys, which is a larger change to `build_table_schema` than this needs.
